Slide 1

Mediastinal diseases

Dr. Alaa Ibrahim Alghamedi MBBS, MPH, FRCSC

Thoracic surgery consultant and assistant professor

Slide 2

Objectives

Slide 3
  • Anatomy
  • Contents of the compartments
  • Imaging
  • Surgical and endoscopic access to the mediastinum
  • Mediastinal conditions:
    • Masses
    • Mediastinal infections
    • Pneumoediastinum

The anatomy

Slide 4
  • It is divided into compartments (Superior compartment, anterior, middle, and posterior)
    • Superior compartment: above the line drawn between the 4th thoracic vertebra and
  • the sternomanubrial junction (angle of Louis)
    • The anterior mediastinum: between the posterior sternum anteriorly and the pericardium posteriorly
    • The middle mediastinum: bound by the pericardium anteriorly and posteriorly
    • The posterior mediastinum: the posterior pericardium anteriorly and the longitudinal
  • spinal ligament posteriorly (vertebral column)
Notes

Mediastinal Anatomy & Compartments

LANDMARK RULE
The pericardium is the practical landmark for compartments: anterior = anterior to pericardium; middle =
pericardium/heart + great vessels, pulmonary arteries/veins, main bronchi, regional lymph nodes; posterior = posterior to pericardium. Some classifications separate a superior mediastinum from the anterior compartment, bounded by the line from the Angle of Louis → superior border of T4.
CompartmentFrequency of massesKey note
AnteriorMost commonThymus, thyroid/parathyroid, germ-cell tumors
Posterior2nd most commonNeurogenic tumors, esophageal lesions
MiddleLeast commonCardiovascular structures, cysts, lymph nodes
Lymph nodes may occur in all compartments and are the most commonly encountered mediastinal mass overall.
  • CT: a thin, fluid-filled structure next to the heart → pericardial cyst. 442
Slide 5
Slide 6
Slide 7
  • The mediastinal tumors most commonly occur in the anterior compartment
  • The middle compartment is the least common location for tumors
  • Lymph nodes can be found in all compartments but most commonly in the anterior
  • compartment (lymphoma). Sarcoidosis is found in the middle compartment
Notes

Mediastinal Lymphadenopathy

CategoryCauses
Primary – malignantLymphoma
Primary – infectiousTB; viral (EBV, CMV, HIV); fungal (aspergillosis — classic STEP 1 question); other bacterial
Primary – inflammatorySarcoidosis, SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, vasculitis
SecondaryMetastatic malignancy, especially lung cancer
WORK-UP BY SUSPICION
TB evaluation / cultures
Rheumatoid factor if appropriate
C-ANCA / P-ANCA for suspected vasculitis
Autoimmune serology (e.g. anti-dsDNA) as indicated
SARCOIDOSIS VS. LYMPHOMA — HIGH-YIELD DISTINCTION
Sarcoidosis: more common in patients of African descent and in females; presents typically in middle age (50s); classically involves the middle compartment. Lymphoma: more characteristically anterior mediastinum, though it can involve the middle compartment.
HIV
HIV can itself cause marked lymphadenopathy, and also predisposes to opportunistic disease causing lymphadenopathy/respiratory infection (e.g. toxoplasmosis, aspergillosis).
  • 45-year-old Black African, SOB, splenomegaly, multiple peribronchial lymphadenopathy → sarcoidosis. 439

Notes

Lesions by Mediastinal Compartment ⭐ Know This Table Well

CompartmentLesions
Anterior / SuperiorThyroid/parathyroid — ectopic parathyroid usually superior, may descend into anterior mediastinum within thymic tissue (persistent ↑PTH after parathyroidectomy → suspect ectopic gland); thyroid usually superior/cervical, can extend anteriorly. Thymus — thymic hyperplasia, thymoma, thymic carcinoma, thymic lymphoma, thymic cyst, thymolipoma. Germ-cell tumors — teratoma, seminoma, NSGCT.
MiddlePulmonary saccular aneurysm; lymphadenopathy; pericardial cyst (congenital; seen more after trauma, e.g. car accidents); bronchogenic cyst (primarily middle, but large lesions may appear posteriorly).
PosteriorSpinal osteophytes; large hiatal hernia; esophageal tumors (leiomyoma, GIST); thoracic duct cystic dilatation; neurogenic tumors (spine, intercostal nerves); ectopic adrenal/paraganglionic tissue.
THORACIC DUCT
Ascends from the diaphragm in the posterior mediastinum, crosses toward the left around T4, then continues into the neck. Cystic enlargement may present as a posterior mediastinal mass.
  • Homogeneous cystic superior mediastinal mass adjacent to the trachea → bronchogenic cyst. 437 ×3

Presentation:

Slide 9
  • Asymptomatic:
    • Incidental finding on imaging
  • Symptomatic:
    • Higher risk of malignancy when symptomatic
    • The symptoms are a result of compression of structures, invasion, or paraneoplastic
  • syndrome
  • When you find a mediastinal mass always ask for:
    • Ach receptor antibodies
    • STM: AFP, B-HCG, LDH
    • For males, get testicular US
  • Young man, incidental anterior mediastinal mass with raised β-hCG and AFP → next step testicular ultrasound. 442
Notes

General Presentation of Mediastinal Tumors

Age groupTypical presentation
AdultsUsually asymptomatic + benign; frequently incidental on imaging. If symptomatic → higher suspicion for malignancy.
ChildrenMore often symptomatic + malignant; imaging is usually performed because symptoms are already present.
Symptoms = Compression / Invasion
Structure involvedSymptom
TracheaDyspnea / respiratory symptoms
Recurrent laryngeal nerveHoarseness
EsophagusDysphagia
PericardiumPericardial effusion ± tamponade physiology
PleuraPleural effusion
Chest wall / pleuraPleuritic chest pain
May also produce paraneoplastic syndromes via hormones/neurotransmitters or electrolyte abnormalities.
⭐ ANTERIOR MEDIASTINAL MASS — CRITICAL WORK-UP (MEMORIZE)
Acetylcholine receptor antibodies — screen for myasthenia gravis associated with thymoma
LDH → lymphoma
AFP → germ-cell tumors
β-hCG → germ-cell tumors
Testicular ultrasound in males — rule out primary testicular GCT with mediastinal metastasis

Imaging

Slide 10
  • Chest x-ray
  • CT Chest: the most important modality
  • MRI:
    • Superior to the CT when it comes to assessing for vascular or structural invasion
    • Helps in differentiating solid vs cystic lesions
    • MRI is ESSENTIAL in assessing posterior compartment tumors: neurogenic tumors with intraspinal components.
  • PET/PET CT: Important for lymphoma staging
  • EUS +/- EBUS: done by the endoscopist
Notes

Imaging of Mediastinal Masses

ModalityRole
Chest X-rayCommon first investigation, particularly in symptomatic patients
Contrast CT chest⭐ Gold standard — main investigation for defining mediastinal masses
MRILocal invasion, vascular involvement, cystic vs. solid, neurogenic tumors, and suspected spinal canal extension / dumbbell tumor
PETNot routine for every mass; useful for lymphoma, thymic carcinoma. Not required for germ-cell tumors.
EBUS & EUS
TechniqueDescription
EBUSEndobronchial ultrasound; bronchoscope with ultrasound capability; visualizes/biopsies peribronchial/mediastinal lymph nodes
EUSEndoscopic ultrasound; gastroscope with ultrasound tip; visualizes/biopsies lesions adjacent to the esophagus
ESOPHAGEAL LEIOMYOMA
Usually submucosal. Avoid biopsy if imaging strongly suggests leiomyoma — biopsy may make later surgical resection difficult. Ultrasound is useful for defining submucosal lesions such as leiomyoma/GIST.

Surgical access to the mediastinum

Slide 11
  • Anterior mediastinum:
    • VATS
    • Robotic surgery (RATS)
    • Median sternotomy
    • Chamberlin procedure (anterior mediastinotomy)
  • Middle mediastinum:
    • Cervical mediastinoscopy
    • Extended cervical mediastinoscopy
    • Chamberlin procedure (anterior mediastinotomy)
    • VATS
    • RATS
  • Posterior mediastinum:
    • Thoracotomy
    • VATS
    • RATS
Notes

Surgical Access — Terminology Only

TermMeaning
VATSVideo-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery
RATSRobotic-Assisted Thoracic Surgery
ThoracotomyOpen thoracic incision
Chamberlain procedureHistorical anterior mediastinotomy; used for station 5 (aortopulmonary window) node sampling; now largely replaced
Cervical mediastinoscopyCervical incision; plane along trachea; scope passed to biopsy paratracheal lymph nodes
  • Biopsy of an anterior mediastinal mass → CT-guided biopsy (mediastinoscopy reaches the middle/paratracheal nodes, not the anterior mediastinum). 436 ×2

Select lesions we will talk about

Slide 12
  • Thymic lesions
  • Germ cell tumors
  • Middle compartment lesions
  • Neurogenic tumors

Thymus

Slide 13
  • Thymomas: associated with myasthenia gravis, agammaglobulinemia, and red
  • blood cell aplasia
  • Thymic cancers
  • Thymic hyperplasia
  • Thymic cysts
  • Thymic carcinoid
  • Thymic lipoma
Notes

Thymic Lesions & Myasthenia Gravis

Most clinically important thymic lesions: thymoma and thymic hyperplasia.

THYMOMA — PARANEOPLASTIC ASSOCIATIONS
Most common: Myasthenia gravis. Hematologic: hypogammaglobulinemia, red-cell aplasia/bone-marrow suppression. ⭐ Identify associated hematologic disease before thymectomy — significant perioperative bleeding/complications may occur.

Myasthenia Gravis

Slide 14
  • Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disorder that affects skeletal muscles.
    • MG is caused by IgG antibodies directed against the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (AChR) complex of the motor end plate.
  • Clinical symptoms range from intermittent ocular weakness to severe generalized muscle weakness to debilitating respiratory depression.
  • This disease is primarily managed by neurologists with anticholinesterase agents (pyridostigmine and neostigmine) and immunomodulating therapies (commonly corticosteroids and azathioprine).
Notes

Myasthenia Gravis — Pathophysiology & Features

Autoantibodies against postsynaptic ACh receptors → ↓ functional receptors → impaired neuromuscular transmission → weakness. Clinical features: progressive/fatigable weakness, ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia. Respiratory arrest risk = respiratory muscle weakness (mechanical failure) or bulbar weakness (poor secretion control/drooling).

DiseaseSiteKey feature
Myasthenia GravisPostsynapticAnti-AChR antibodies; fatigable weakness
Lambert-EatonPresynapticAnti-voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channel antibodies
Guillain-BarréPeripheral nerveAscending weakness → may progress to respiratory failure; linked to Campylobacter jejuni, occasionally post-vaccination
Myasthenia Gravis — Treatment
CategoryAgents / approach
SymptomaticAcetylcholinesterase inhibitors — pyridostigmine, neostigmine (ACh persists longer in synaptic cleft)
ImmunosuppressionSteroids; azathioprine and other agents
Myasthenic crisisPlasmapheresis (removes circulating antibodies, faster/immediate) vs. IVIG (repeated doses, slower onset)
PREOPERATIVE OPTIMIZATION (HIGH-RISK MG)
Admit → 2 doses IVIG → operate approximately 7 days later after optimization.
  • Ptosis, diplopia, positive Tensilon test and a homogeneous anterior mediastinal mass → myasthenia gravis with thymoma. 439 ×4
Slide 15Myasthenia Gravis
  • Plasmapheresis removes antibodies from the circulation and produces short-term clinical improvement. It is used primarily to stabilize the condition of patients in myasthenic crisis or in patients with refractory disease. The effect of plasmapheresis is rapid with improvement occurring within days of treatment (lasts for few weeks)
  • Alternative approaches include intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) that can be infused to bind anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies
  • The majority of patients with myasthenia gravis who undergo thymectomy improve or
  • have complete remission of their disease over several years.
  • There is strong evidence to also support thymectomy in the non-non-thymomatous myasthenic patient
Notes

Myasthenia Gravis + Thymectomy

MG + THYMOMA → THYMECTOMY (COMPLETE THYMOMA REMOVAL)
Post-thymectomy response in roughly thirds: ⅓ medication-independent/remission; ⅓ improvement with reduced medication; ⅓ little/no significant change.

MG without thymoma: medical therapy often controls symptoms, but prolonged immunosuppression risks infections, HPA-axis suppression/adrenal insufficiency (chronic steroids), and organ toxicity/secondary malignancy including lymphoma and skin cancer (long-term immunosuppressants). Thymectomy can benefit selected non-thymomatous patients.

SELECTION CRITERIA FOR THYMECTOMY IN NON-THYMOMATOUS MG
Age 18 to <60 years
Symptoms <5 years
Good response to medication
Minimally invasive VATS/robotic thymectomy has reduced surgical burden and expanded use in this group.
  • MG with a 6.5 × 7 cm thymoma → surgical approach keyed VATS thymectomy (complete thymectomy; sternotomy for large invasive tumours). 438 ×3

Germ cell tumors

Slide 16
  • The majority of germ cell tumors originate in the gonads however, 5 to 10% of all germ cell tumors arise within the anterior mediastinum, which represents the second most common site of origin.
    • Teratoma
    • Seminomatous (PMSGCT)
    • Nonseminomatous (PMNSGCT) germ cell tumors
Notes

Mediastinal Germ-Cell Tumors

Usually arise from gonadal germ cells (~90%, testicle/ovary), but extragonadal tumors occur. Approximately 5–10% are described in the anterior mediastinum, an important extragonadal site (a smaller proportion arise abdominally/peritoneally). Main types: teratoma, seminoma, NSGCT.

Teratomas

Slide 17
  • Unlike malignant germ cell tumors, which almost uniformly occur in the male
  • population, mature teratomas occur with equal frequency in both genders.
  • While reported in all age groups, the vast majority present in infancy or childhood with chest pain being the most common symptom, followed by dyspnea, and cough.
  • Occasionally, a cystic component can become infected producing local or
  • systemic symptoms.
  • Rarely, cyst contents may rupture into the pleural space or tracheobronchial tree,
  • the latter resulting in the expectoration of hair or sebum which is pathognomonic.
  • Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic tumors can be incidental findings on
  • chest radiographs or CT scans which is more common in the adult population.
Slide 18
  • CT scan usually demonstrates a mass
  • Approximately half of these tumors radiographically demonstrate calcification and on occasion recognizable bone or teeth are present
  • Serum tumor markers (STM), alpha fetoprotein (AFP) and the beta subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin (HCG) should be obtained but are usually normal with these radiographic findings
  • Benign teratomas are not responsive to radiation or chemotherapy. In the usual situation of typical CT findings with normal STM, complete surgical excision is therefore recommended without biopsy
  • Anterior mass with calcification, teeth and bone, normal AFP/β-hCG → teratoma. 442

Seminomatous germ cell tumors (PMSGCT)

Slide 19
  • Histologically these neoplasms appear similar to their testicular germ cell tumors
  • Exclusively in young adult males, 20 to 40 years of age
  • Symptoms such as chest pain, dyspnea, and cough develop
  • Chest CT characteristically reveals a bulky, lobulated, but homogenous mass with only
  • occasional invasion of adjacent structures.
  • Metastatic disease at the time of diagnosis can occur to the cervical lymph nodes, lungs,
  • liver, or bone.
  • 40-year-old man, anterior mediastinal mass, negative markers, homogeneous on CT → seminoma. 439
Slide 20
  • Patients with pure PMSGCT usually have normal STM
  • Cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy regimens such as BEP (bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin
  • In contrast to PMNSGCT, any residual anterior mediastinal mass following chemotherapy
  • usually represents tumor necrosis only and therefore surgery is not indicated.
  • Young man, fever, night sweats, weight loss, heterogeneous anterior mass, Reed-Sternberg cells (Hodgkin lymphoma) → chemotherapy (not surgery). 437 ×6

Nonseminomatous Germ Cell Cancer (PMNSGT)

Slide 21
  • PMNSGCT have an overall worse prognosis and therefore have been categorized as “poor
  • risk”
  • Types:
    • yolk sac cancer (most common)
    • embryonal carcinoma
    • choriocarcinoma (least common)
    • typically mixed with some form of teratomatous pathology ranging from mature teratoma, to teratoma with immature elements
  • CT scans usually demonstrate a large heterogeneous mass with occasional evidence of necrosis and hemorrhage. Local invasion into the lung, great veins, or pericardium is common.
Notes

NSGCT — Surgical Considerations

Usually not operated on first (often large/invasive) — chemotherapy first improves resectability. A rare small lesion (<4 cm, no invasion) may sometimes be directly excised (diagnostic + therapeutic). Operations may be major: sternotomy, trapdoor incision, combined approaches, major vascular reconstruction, occasionally cardiopulmonary bypass.

OPERABILITY VS. RESECTABILITY
Operability = whether the patient can physiologically tolerate surgery. Resectability = whether the tumor can
technically/oncologically be removed. Roughly 20–40% may have metastases at presentation (commonly lung, liver); metastasis is not automatically a contraindication to surgery. NCCN criteria guide selection. Prognosis is poorer than gonadal disease, with failure typically from systemic/metastatic progression rather than local effects.
Slide 22
  • STM is an essential component of clinical evaluation as serum AFP elevation is diagnostic of a PMNSGCT obviating the need for histologic confirmation.
  • Metastatic disease is present in 20 to 25% of cases prior to chemotherapy with lung being the
  • most common site of metastases followed by cervical lymph nodes, liver, bone, and CNS.
  • Appropriate therapy begins with four cycles of cisplatin-based chemotherapy: BEP risk of O2
  • toxicity
  • Optimally STM normalize and surgery is planned after adequate functional and hematologic recovery, which usually occurs after 6 weeks following completion of chemotherapy
  • Growing teratoma: paradoxical growth of a cystic mass causing symptomatic compression of adjacent organs associated with rapid normalization of serum tumor markers during chemotherapy. In these cases, chemotherapy should be discontinued and surgery undertaken.
  • NSGCT on chemo: mass enlarging while markers normalize → growing teratoma syndrome. 442
  • 18-year-old on chemo for an anterior mediastinal mass, worse SOB after the 2nd cycle with normalizing markers → nonseminoma (growing teratoma component). 439
Notes

Comparison: Teratoma vs. Seminoma vs. NSGCT

TeratomaSeminomaNSGCT
EpidemiologyAny age/sex; often symptomatic in younger patientsMale disease; age 20–40More aggressive; mixed with teratoma frequently
CT appearanceHair, fat, teeth (mature)Homogeneous; less necrosis, less invasion, less metastasisHeterogeneous; more necrosis, more invasion, more nodal & distant metastasis
Tumor markersNormal (pure teratoma)Usually normalElevated AFP and/or β-hCG
TreatmentComplete surgical excision; chemo/radio ineffective for mature teratomaNon-surgical: cisplatin-based chemo (BEP); radiotherapy less usedNeoadjuvant platinum-based chemo (BEP) → surgical resection
CLASSIC TERATOMA PEARL
CT shows hair/teeth + normal tumor markers → usually excise without biopsy. Biopsy is reserved for the one situation where teratoma is seen together with NSGCT.
RUPTURED TERATOMA
Can cause marked local inflammation (may produce acid) and rupture into the pleural space (effusion/inflammatory reaction, empyema) or airway (patient may cough up hair or teeth). Initial approach: antibiotics, chest tube if pleural contamination, CT chest, bronchoscopy to assess airway communication. Early surgery if fresh/technically feasible; if severe adhesions have formed, stabilize and delay surgery — dense adhesions from chest inflammation make later operations technically difficult.
⭐ BEP REGIMEN — HIGHLY TESTABLE
Bleomycin, Etoposide, Cisplatin. Bleomycin toxicity: pulmonary fibrosis; high oxygen exposure can precipitate/worsen bleomycin lung injury. An alternative platinum regimen without bleomycin may be used when pulmonary toxicity is a concern.
⭐ GROWING TERATOMA SYNDROME
During chemotherapy for mixed NSGCT, the malignant component dies but the chemo-resistant teratoma continues to enlarge — tumor markers improve while the mass grows and compressive symptoms worsen. Management: stop chemotherapy, proceed to prompt surgical resection. Teratoma is not effectively treated by chemotherapy.

Middle compartment

Slide 23
  • Bronchogenic and esophageal cysts:
    • Bronchogenic cysts are commonly symptomatic in contrast to esophageal cysts,
  • which are asymptomatic.
    • Complete excision is the treatment of choice and is indicated in most patients for increasing size or treatment of symptoms or complications.
  • Pericardial cysts:
    • Congenital
    • Surgical resection has been the preferred treatment over aspiration particularly for enlarging or symptomatic pericardial cysts
Notes

Cystic Lesions

Bronchogenic & Esophageal Duplication Cysts

Both arise from developmental abnormalities during embryologic separation of the foregut into trachea + esophagus. Abnormal

isolated, epithelial-lined tissue (usually no luminal communication) may collect fluid over time, enlarge, or become infected.

CystLocation
Bronchogenic cystMiddle mediastinum
Esophageal duplication cystPosterior mediastinum
Symptoms depend on size/location: cough, dysphagia, or fever/sepsis-type symptoms if infected. Indications for excision: increasing size, symptomatic, or complicated/infected. Pericardial Cyst
Usually congenital; can also occur after trauma. Approximately 70% right-sided, 30% left-sided.
TREATMENT
⭐ Excision. Simple aspiration is usually inadequate because the cyst tends to reaccumulate.
  • Cough + mild dysphagia, enlarged right thyroid lobe, CXR mass in the superior mediastinum (retrosternal goitre) → CT chest and neck. 438 ×11

Neurogenic tumors

Slide 24
  • Neurogenic tumors in the adult are commonly of nerve sheath origin and the majority are benign:
    • Nerve sheath tumors comprise one fifth of all mediastinal tumors: schwannomas, neurofibromas, and malignant schwannomas (neurogenic sarcomas).
  • Children and young adults are more prone to tumors of the autonomic ganglia, which are frequently malignant.
    • Tumors arising from autonomic ganglia are classified into three histologic types: ganglioneuroma, ganglioneuroblastoma, and neuroblastoma.
  • Mediastinal pheochromocytomas comprise less than 2% of all pheochromocytomas. Their presentation is consistent with overproduction of catecholamines, resulting in paroxysmal or sustained hypertension. Diagnosis is by measurement of urinary catecholamines and their metabolites.
  • Von Recklinghausen’s neurofibromatosis is the only known predisposing factor for benign and malignant
  • neurogenic tumors.
  • Surgery plays a dominant role in the treatment of for neurogenic tumors.
  • Intraspinal extension of neurogenic tumors must be recognized preoperatively and requires a combined posterior spinal and thoracic approach for safe resection (dumbbell tumors).
  • Asymptomatic young man, rounded left paravertebral (posterior) mass at T12 → neurofibroma (neurogenic tumour). 437 ×9
Notes

Neurogenic Tumors

Age groupBehaviorCommon types
AdultsMajority benign; often incidental, or presenting with back painSchwannoma, neurofibroma, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor
ChildrenMore likely malignant/autonomic ganglion tumors; may be hormonally activeGanglioneuroma, ganglioneuroblastoma, neuroblastoma
⭐ DUMBBELL NEUROGENIC TUMOR
Tumor extends through an intervertebral foramen into the spinal canal (a "dumbbell in gym" appearance). MRI is essential preoperatively to identify spinal extension — blind thoracic resection could cause spinal cord/nerve injury. If spinal extension is present, coordinate with the spine/neurosurgical team.
MEDIASTINAL PARAGANGLIOMA / ECTOPIC PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA
Ectopic adrenal/paraganglionic tissue may remain in the thorax and secrete catecholamines → severe hypertension, tachycardia, severe headache, panic-attack/MI-like symptoms, hypertensive emergency. Investigation: urinary catecholamine metabolites (VMA). Treatment: surgical excision after appropriate diagnosis/preparation.
  • Headache and arm weakness with a posterior mediastinal mass → spinal MRI (rule out intraspinal "dumbbell" extension). 439

Mediastinitis: Anatomic considerations

Slide 25
  • Deep cervical fascial layers separate the neck into three compartments:
    • Retrovisceral
    • Pretracheal
    • Perivascular
  • Each of these spaces can communicate with the mediastinum.
  • The most common pathway is via the retrovisceral space with caudal extension of infection into
  • the posterior mediastinum.
  • Another route extends anteriorly through the pretracheal space in an inferior, retrosternal direction. This can lead to pleural and/or pericardial space involvement, the latter producing purulent pericarditis and even pericardial tamponade.
  • The last route of extension is into the perivascular space within the carotid sheath, potentially
  • leading to cranial nerve palsies and massive hemorrhage from vessel erosion.
Notes

Mediastinitis

Inflammation/infection of mediastinal tissues. Important because cervical fascial planes communicate directly with the mediastinum — head/neck infection can descend into the chest.

CauseDetail
Dental/oral infectionEspecially poor dentition/hygiene; long-term care/psychiatric patients
Pharyngitis / perforation—
TonsillitisEspecially in immunocompromised patients
PostoperativeAfter sternotomy
Cervical Fascial Pathways to Mediastinum
SpaceLocationNote
PretrachealAnterior to tracheaCommunicates with anterior mediastinum/pleural spaces
RetrovisceralPosterior to esophagus⭐ Most common descending pathway; descends toward posterior mediastinum
Perivascular / carotidAround carotid vesselsLess common but dangerous — mycotic aneurysm, carotid blowout, stroke-like complications
⭐ ACUTE NECROTIZING MEDIASTINITIS
Life-threatening infection, analogous to necrotizing fasciitis of the mediastinum. Risk settings: descending oral/neck infection, post-sternotomy; comorbidities include diabetes/poor glycemic control, hypertension, smoking, obesity. Mortality ~50% even with antibiotics.
Clinical clue: fever + hypotension + severe tachycardia + bilateral pleural effusions + poor dentition/recent neck infection → urgent CT chest.
Treatment requires all of: broad antibiotics, drainage, urgent surgical debridement — often repeated, e.g. return to OR roughly every 48 h with ongoing necrosis. Antibiotics alone are insufficient.
  • Fever, chest pain, neck swelling after a dental infection, air in the mediastinum → descending necrotizing mediastinitis. 442
Slide 26

Acute necrotizing mediastinitis (ANM):

Slide 27
  • Life threatening
  • Source: Odontogenic, peritonsillar, or other pharyngeal infections
  • Post op from a sternotomy
  • It may also result from iatrogenic oropharyngeal perforation, thoracic esophageal perforation, paraesophageal hernia with intrathoracic gastric perforation, cervical trauma, sternoclavicular joint infection, extension of retroperitoneal pancreatic infection into the chest, iatrogenic infusion into the mediastinum via improperly placed central venous line, and illicit intravenous drug administration.
Slide 28
  • Diagnosis: CT neck and chest- fluid collections, air bubbles, thickening of the tissues
  • Treatment of ANM begins with intravenous administration of a broad-spectrum antibiotic, such as piperacillin-tazobactam, which would be expected to cover both aerobes and anaerobes of oropharyngeal origin and urgent debridement and drainage

Pneumomediastinum

Slide 29
  • Pneumomediastinum refers to the presence of air in the mediastinal space.
  • The most common source is extension of air from the lung.
  • Any cause of alveolar rupture, such as deep respiratory maneuvers, asthma, vomiting esp in pregnancy, mechanical ventilation (barotrauma), or thoracic trauma, may lead to passage of air towards the hilum and the mediastinum.
  • Traumatic rupture of the trachea or main bronchi and esophageal perforation are less common but more serious causes of pneumomediastinum.
  • Coughing then neck pain, pneumomediastinum → extension of air from the lung. 441
Notes

Pneumomediastinum

Associated with DKA + vomiting, hyperemesis gravidarum in pregnancy, mechanical ventilation (barotrauma), severe coughing/vomiting. Most common source is lung/alveolar air leak, not tracheal or esophageal rupture — air dissects along tissue planes via the path of least resistance.

UNCOMPLICATED PNEUMOMEDIASTINUM
Oxygen, analgesia, observation/treat precipitating cause. The key task is identifying the minority with life-threatening esophageal or airway injury.
Notes

Clinical Safety Point — Immunosuppression / HIV

Severe lymphadenopathy may relate to HIV itself or an associated opportunistic infection/malignancy. Check immune status when clinically relevant — marked neutropenia/immunosuppression greatly increases operative risk. Pending or positive HIV (or other infectious/immunodeficiency) test results must be communicated to the whole treating team, especially before invasive procedures. HIV patients may have severe lymphadenopathy, severe respiratory infections, and opportunistic infections (TB, toxoplasmosis, aspergillosis, etc.).
Mastery Checklist
1 Compartments are defined relative to the pericardium; anterior masses are most common, lymph nodes occur in all compartments.
2 Sarcoidosis favors the middle compartment (African descent, female, 50s); lymphoma favors the anterior
compartment.
3 Any anterior mediastinal mass in a male needs AChR antibodies, LDH, AFP, β-hCG, and testicular ultrasound.
4 Contrast CT chest is the gold standard; MRI is required whenever a dumbbell tumor (spinal extension) is suspected; PET is not routine for germ-cell tumors.
5 Teratoma: hair/teeth/fat on CT + normal markers → excise without biopsy; biopsy only if NSGCT is also suspected.
6 Seminoma is homogeneous with normal markers, treated with BEP chemotherapy (non-surgical); NSGCT is
heterogeneous with elevated AFP/β-hCG, treated with neoadjuvant chemo then resection.
7 Growing teratoma syndrome: markers improve but mass enlarges during chemo → stop chemo, resect promptly.
8 In MG, identify hematologic paraneoplastic disease before thymectomy to avoid perioperative bleeding complications.
9 Myasthenic crisis: plasmapheresis acts faster than IVIG.
10 Lambert-Eaton is presynaptic (Ca²⁺ channel antibodies); MG is postsynaptic (AChR antibodies).
11 The retrovisceral space is the most common route for descending neck infection to reach the mediastinum.
12 Acute necrotizing mediastinitis needs antibiotics + drainage + urgent debridement — antibiotics alone are not enough (~50% mortality).
13 Most pneumomediastinum arises from an alveolar air leak, not esophageal or tracheal rupture — but always rule those out.
14 Non-contained esophageal perforation (Boerhaave) requires urgent surgery; contained perforation can be managed conservatively.
15 A major air leak that persists despite a chest tube signals tracheobronchial injury → bronchoscopy is the next step.
16 Pericardial cysts should be excised, not aspirated — aspiration alone tends to recur.

Treatment

Slide 30
  • If the patient is asymptomatic and there is no concern for airway or esophageal injury: no treatment necessary
  • Esophageal perforation:
    • life-threatening emergency
    • If contained, treat conservatively with NPO and IV antibiotic
    • If not contained: NPO, IV antibiotics, chest tube placement, OR for repair and drainage
  • Airway injury:
    • Traumatic or iatrogenic
    • Suspected when there is a constant airleak from the chest tube with a nonexpanding lung on x-ray
    • Intubation using bronchoscopy: assess the airway and intubate beyond the injury
    • Requires surgery for airway repair
Notes

Esophageal Perforation / Boerhaave Syndrome

Boerhaave syndrome = spontaneous esophageal rupture, classically after forceful vomiting.

INITIAL MANAGEMENT
NPO, IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, endoscopic/scope assessment as appropriate.
TypeManagement
ContainedSealed/localized contamination → conservative: NPO, IV fluids, antibiotics, close reassessment (~72 h)
Non-containedFree leak/ongoing contamination → very high mortality → urgent surgery (primary repair when possible; resection in selected severe cases)
TRACHEOBRONCHIAL / AIRWAY INJURY
Classic scenario: chest tube inserted for pneumothorax, lung fails to re-expand, continuous major air leak (ventilator tidal volume escapes through the tube). Adding another chest tube will not fix a major airway disruption. Next step: bronchoscopy to define the injury; airway/intubation may need to be performed under bronchoscopic guidance.
  • Stable, pneumomediastinum, endoscopy shows a contained oesophageal leak → NPO + IV antibiotics (conservative). 441
